questions.prompt: A streaming variance computed as (sum_sq - n*mean^2)/(n-1) is run on values around 1e9. What is the typical symptom?
options: An empty optional returned for large inputs
A slightly slower but still exact result
An integer overflow exception thrown at run time
A wildly inaccurate or even negative variance
questions.explanation: Two huge, nearly equal numbers are subtracted, so rounding error dominates.

questions.prompt: Why prefer static_assert(std::is_floating_point_v<T>) over documenting 'T must be floating point' in a comment?
options: It makes the generated code run noticeably faster at run time
It lets integer types be used safely inside the template
Comments are not allowed anywhere inside template code
The compiler enforces it and reports your message at instantiation
questions.explanation: A checked assumption fails loudly where it is violated.

questions.prompt: Which makes 'template <class T> T clamp_to(T, T, T);' with its body in util.cpp link for int and double?
options: Declare the function inline in main.cpp only, and keep the body in util.cpp
Link the program with -lstdc++ so that the template symbols resolve
Add const to every parameter in the declaration and the definition
template int clamp_to<int>(int,int,int); and the same for double in util.cpp
questions.explanation: Explicit instantiation emits the specializations in util.cpp; putting the body in the header is the other fix.

Write a templated function describe(T) that returns "integer" for integral types, "real" for floating-point types and "other" otherwise, using if constexpr. Why would a plain if not work if one branch calls std::sqrt(x)?
rubric: Uses if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) ... else if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<T>) ... else ...
A plain if still compiles every branch for every T, so std::sqrt(x) must be valid even for strings.
Notes the untaken branches are discarded, not just skipped at run time.
